raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the lifesaving benefit of defibrillation while avoiding the long-term liabilities of transvenous leads. Early human feasibility work showed that ventricular fibrillation could be sensed and terminated using a parasternal lead and lateral pulse generator, establishing the concept of a wholly extrathoracic ICD system [1,2]. Subsequent pivotal and registry data confirmed high defibrillation efficacy and acceptable short-term safety, leading to broad adoption in patients who require protection from sudden cardiac death but do not need chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP) [3-6].

The principal advantage of the S-ICD is anatomic: no lead traverses the venous system, tricuspid valve, or endocardium. This is attractive for young patients, those with limited venous access, prior device infection, congenital heart disease, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, or high anticipated lifetime lead-failure risk [7,8]. Comparative evidence has matured. In the randomized PRAETORIAN trial, the S-ICD was noninferior to transvenous ICD therapy for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [9]. Observational comparisons similarly suggest fewer lead-related complications and systemic infections with S-ICD therapy, balanced by the absence of ATP and a different inappropriate-shock profile [10,11].

Patient selection remains central. The best candidates are those with primary or secondary prevention ICD indications, sinus rhythm or limited pacing needs, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias expected to be polymorphic or fast enough to require shocks rather than ATP [12]. Patients with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia likely to respond to ATP, established pacing indications, or anticipated resynchronization needs are usually better served by transvenous or extravascular pacing-capable systems. Pre-implant electrocardiographic screening is essential because S-ICD sensing relies on far-field subcutaneous signals; screening identifies patients at risk of T-wave oversensing, low QRS amplitude, or morphology changes that may compromise discrimination [13,14].

Implant technique has evolved. Early three-incision approaches have largely been replaced by two-incision techniques, and intermuscular generator placement between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi improves cosmesis, comfort, and system stability [15,16]. Defibrillation testing has traditionally been performed because the system is extravascular and dependent on generator position and shock vector; however, accumulating data support omission in selected patients when implant position is optimal and patient risk from testing is high [17,18]. Procedural complications include hematoma, pocket pain, erosion, infection, lead migration, and early sensing problems; most are manageable, but meticulous tunneling, anchoring, and pocket creation are important [19].

Inappropriate shocks were an early limitation, most often caused by T-wave oversensing, supraventricular tachycardia, myopotentials, or low-amplitude signals. Contemporary programming with dual zones, conditional discrimination, improved sensing algorithms, and software filters has substantially reduced inappropriate therapy [20,21]. The UNTOUCHED study, focused on contemporary programming in primary-prevention patients with reduced ejection fraction, demonstrated low inappropriate-shock rates while maintaining effective conversion of ventricular arrhythmias [22]. Nevertheless, exercise, postural changes, bundle-branch block, and dynamic repolarization abnormalities can alter sensing; repeat screening or vector reprogramming is sometimes required [23].

The absence of ATP is the most important functional limitation. Many ICD shocks are avoidable in transvenous systems through ATP for organized ventricular tachycardia. For patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and recurrent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, this difference can meaningfully affect quality of life and health-care utilization [24]. Conversely, in inherited channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, dialysis patients, and younger primary-prevention populations, shock-only therapy may be acceptable because the dominant risk is ventricular fibrillation or very fast polymorphic tachycardia [25-27].

Infection management is another major consideration. Because the S-ICD has no intravascular component, pocket infection is less likely to progress to endocarditis, and extraction is generally simpler than removal of chronically implanted transvenous leads [28]. This feature is especially relevant after extraction for infection, in patients on hemodialysis, and in those with limited venous access. However, the larger generator and lateral pocket can be associated with discomfort, particularly in small or thin patients [29].

Future directions include better integration with leadless pacing, modular ATP-capable systems, longer battery longevity, smaller generators, improved morphology discrimination, and refined strategies for defibrillation testing. The S-ICD has shifted ICD decision-making from a default transvenous approach to a patient-specific assessment of pacing need, arrhythmia substrate, infection risk, venous anatomy, and lifetime lead management. For appropriately selected patients, contemporary evidence supports the S-ICD as an effective, durable, and often preferable alternative to transvenous defibrillator therapy [30].
